walkthroughs.body_html:
Paper 2: Exploring Effects and Impact — a core area of GCSE English Language.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Paper 2: Exploring Effects and Impact brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Paper 2: Exploring Effects and Impact.

mcqs.q: What is a speech act according to Searle/Austin?
options: A speech act is a performance or a play.
Voiced sounds use the lips; voiceless sounds use the tongue.
An utterance that performs an action — promising, ordering, apologising, declaring. Speech acts have locutionary (what's said), illocutionary (intended force) and perlocutionary (effect) dimensions.
A speech act is any time someone speaks.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between voiced and voiceless sounds?
options: Voiced sounds use the lips; voiceless sounds use the tongue.
Transitive verbs end in -ed and intransitive in -ing.
Voiced sounds are produced with vocal-fold vibration (/b/, /d/, /g/, /z/); voiceless sounds without it (/p/, /t/, /k/, /s/). You can feel the difference by putting a hand on your throat.
Voiced sounds are loud and voiceless sounds are whispered.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between transitive and intransitive verbs?
options: Transitive verbs take a direct object ('she ate the cake'); intransitive verbs don't ('she slept'). Some verbs are both depending on use ('she ran' / 'she ran the company').
Voiced sounds use the lips; voiceless sounds use the tongue.
Transitive verbs end in -ed and intransitive in -ing.
Transitive verbs are action verbs and intransitive are linking verbs.
